To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the risk of emesis is a continuous variable; (2) the risk of nausea and vomiting is related to the risk of emetogenicity; (3) the use of anti-emetic prophylaxis can be tailored according to the risk of nausea, and vomiting; (4) antiemetic prophylaxis should include a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, a corticosteroid, and an additional antiemetic, as appropriate.

(1) the antiemetic management of chemotherapy-induced nausea and emesis is not always in keeping with the available guidelines; (2) a more simplified approach to antiemetic management may be helpful; (3) the creation of a consensus document that includes a simplified approach to anti-emetic management is feasible; and (4) the use of a consensus statement and a simplified approach may improve the management of chemotherapy-induced emesis.

the use of anti-emetic agents should be based on emetic risk, that anti-emetic agents are most effective when given before chemotherapy administration, and that the most effective anti-emetic regimens include a combination of agents.

the use of anti-emetic guidelines in the treatment of patients receiving chemotherapy is a good idea, but it is not being done as often as it should.
the use of anti-emetics is a complex and challenging area of clinical practice, which is why this guideline has been developed.
the most effective antiemetic regimen is the one that is most effective for the individual patient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have tried to simplify the guidelines to make them more practical and easier for the oncology nurse and practitioner to use in the everyday practice of chemotherapy.
antiemetic management is a process, not an acute event.
we have tried to create a document that will be more useful in everyday practice and that is based on available evidence and consensus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

antiemetics are not interchangeable and that the selection of an appropriate agent is based on a patient's risk for emesis and the timing of that risk, and not simply on the patient's age, gender, or weight.
we need to view the entire treatment period, not just the day of chemotherapy administration, when selecting appropriate antiemetic therapy.
we should be using antiemetic agents appropriately to help our patients avoid nausea and vomiting.
